title: Ramus repertus. Rogus Miseni. Vestibulum Orci
titleEn: The Bough Found, Misenus's Pyre and the Threshold of the Dead — Aeneid VI.190–294
part: The Bough Found, Misenus's Pyre and the Threshold of the Dead (VI.190–294)
about: Hardly has Aeneas finished his prayer when two doves, his mother's birds, come down in front of him. He asks them to guide him, and they fly on a little at a time until, at the reeking mouth of Avernus, they rise and settle on a tree where gold gleams among the green, like mistletoe in midwinter. Aeneas breaks off the bough, though it clings, and carries it to the Sibyl. Meanwhile the Trojans give Misenus his funeral: the pyre, the washing of the body, the torch held with faces turned away, the bones gathered into a bronze urn, and a mound under the headland that still bears his name. Then Aeneas does what the Sibyl ordered. At a deep cave by a black lake, whose fumes no bird can fly over, she sacrifices black bullocks and calls on Hecate, and Aeneas offers victims to Night, to Earth, to Proserpina and to the king of the dead. At dawn the ground groans and Hecate's hounds howl; the Sibyl drives off the uninitiated, tells Aeneas to draw his sword and be brave, and plunges into the cave with Aeneas at her side. The poet asks the gods of the dead for leave to tell what he has heard, and the two go on through the dark like travellers in a wood under a clouded moon. At the entrance wait Grief and Cares, Disease, Old Age, Fear, Hunger, Want, Death, Sleep, War and Discord; an elm where empty Dreams cling under the leaves; and the old monsters, Centaurs, Scyllas, Briareus, the Hydra, the Chimaera, Gorgons, Harpies and Geryon. Aeneas draws his sword on them, and would have hacked at empty air if the Sibyl had not told him they were bodiless shades.

sentences.t:
Vix ea fatus erat, geminae cum forte columbae
ipsa sub ora viri caelo venere volantes,
et viridi sedere solo.
sentences.l:
Scarcely had he spoken these things, when by chance twin doves
right beneath the face of the man from the sky came flying,
and on the green ground settled.
sentences.i: Hardly had he spoken when, as it chanced, a pair of doves came flying down out of the sky right before his eyes and settled on the green grass.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Vix… cum' is the so-called inverted 'cum': the main clause ('vix ea fatus erat', 'scarcely had he said this') gives the moment, and the 'cum' clause, in the indicative, brings the sudden event. 'Fatus erat' is the pluperfect of the deponent 'for', 'speak'. 'Ipsa sub ora viri' is 'right under the man's face'; 'caelo' is an ablative of the place from which, 'from the sky', with no preposition. 'Venere' and 'sedere' are the short perfects in '-ere' for '-erunt'. 'Viridi… solo' frames the end of the clause, 'on the green ground'. Doves are the birds of Venus, Aeneas's mother, as the next line says.

sentences.t:
Tum maximus heros
maternas agnoscit aves, laetusque precatur:
sentences.l:
Then the greatest hero
his mother's birds recognises, and glad he prays:
sentences.i: Then the great hero knew them for his mother's birds, and joyfully he prayed:
sentences.n: 'Maximus heros' is Aeneas. 'Maternas… aves' is 'the maternal birds', an adjective doing the work of a genitive, 'his mother's birds': the dove was sacred to Venus. 'Agnoscit' is a historic present (the Latin Library prints 'agnovit', a perfect, with no change of sense). 'Laetus' is an adjective where English would use an adverb, 'gladly', a habit of Latin verse. 'Precatur' is a deponent; the colon opens his prayer.

sentences.t:
“Este duces, O, si qua via est, cursumque per auras
dirigite in lucos, ubi pinguem dives opacat
ramus humum.
sentences.l:
“Be my guides, O, if any way there is, and your course through the air
steer into the groves where on the fat ground the rich
bough casts its shade.
sentences.i: “Be my guides, if there is any way, and steer your flight through the air into the groves where the precious bough throws its shade on the rich earth.
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Aeneas's prayer, which runs to 197. 'Este' is the plural imperative of 'sum', 'be', with 'duces' as predicate, 'be guides'. The interjection 'O' stands loose in the line, a cry rather than part of an address. 'Si qua via est' is 'if there is any way', 'qua' being the indefinite after 'si' (as in 'si quis', 'si qua'). 'Dirigite' is the plural imperative, 'steer' (the Latin Library spells it 'derigite'). The last clause is interlaced: 'pinguem… humum' (the fertile ground) encloses 'dives… ramus' (the rich bough), so the bough is set in its ground in the words themselves; 'opacat' is 'shades'. 'Dives' is 'rich' because the bough is gold.

sentences.t:
Tuque, O, dubiis ne defice rebus,
diva parens.
sentences.l:
And you, O, in my wavering fortunes do not fail me,
goddess mother.”
sentences.i: And you, my goddess mother, do not fail me now that my fortunes hang in doubt.”
sentences.n: The print has 'parens. ”Sic', a misprint for 'parens.” Sic', corrected here. The mark closing Aeneas's prayer is set after a space and joined to the next word, so t keeps the print and the mark stands at the head of the next unit, while l and i close the speech after 'parens.'. 'Ne defice' is 'ne' with the imperative, an old and poetic form of prohibition (prose says 'noli deficere'). 'Dubiis… rebus' is 'in doubtful circumstances', a dative or ablative: he does not know where the bough is. 'Diva parens' is Venus, addressed with 'tu', 'you', put first.

sentences.t:
”Sic effatus vestigia pressit,
observans quae signa ferant, quo tendere pergant.
sentences.l:
So having spoken he checked his footsteps,
watching what signs they bring, where to head they go on.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and stood still, watching what signs they would give and which way they would go.
sentences.n: The print has 'parens. ”Sic', a misprint for 'parens.” Sic', corrected here; the mark at the head of t belongs to the prayer just ended, so l and i carry none. 'Effatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'effor', 'having spoken out'. 'Vestigia pressit' is 'pressed his steps', that is checked them and stood still. 'Quae signa ferant' and 'quo tendere pergant' are indirect questions in the present subjunctive after 'observans', 'watching what signs they bring, where they go on to head'; 'tendere' depends on 'pergant'. Watching the flight of birds for an omen is the augur's craft.

sentences.t:
Pascentes illae tantum prodire volando,
quantum acie possent oculi servare sequentum.
sentences.l:
They, feeding, only so far went forward in flight,
as with their sight the eyes could keep them of those following.
sentences.i: They, feeding as they went, flew on only so far ahead as the eyes of one following could keep them in sight.
sentences.n: 'Prodire' is a historical infinitive, an infinitive standing for a finite past verb ('they went forward'), used in quick narrative. 'Pascentes' is 'feeding', stopping to peck as they go. 'Tantum… quantum' is 'only so far… as'. 'Acie' is 'with their sight', the keenness of the eye; 'servare' is 'keep (in view)'. 'Sequentum' is the genitive plural of the participle with the short ending '-um' for '-ium', 'of those following'. 'Possent' is subjunctive because the limit is the doves' own design: they keep within sight on purpose.

sentences.t:
Inde ubi venere ad fauces grave olentis Averni,
tollunt se celeres, liquidumque per aëra lapsae
sedibus optatis geminae super arbore sidunt,
discolor unde auri per ramos aura refulsit.
sentences.l:
Then, when they came to the jaws of foul-smelling Avernus,
they lift themselves swift, and through the clear air gliding
on the wished-for seat the pair upon the tree alight,
from where, different in colour, of gold through the branches a gleam shone out.
sentences.i: Then, when they reached the throat of reeking Avernus, they rose swiftly, glided down through the clear air, and settled side by side where he longed to see them, on the top of the tree from which the gleam of gold, another colour from the leaves, shone out through the boughs.
sentences.n: 'Inde ubi' is 'then, when'. 'Fauces' are 'jaws', 'throat', the narrow mouth of the lake and its cave. 'Grave olentis' is 'heavily smelling', 'grave' being a neuter accusative used as an adverb; Avernus gave off sulphurous fumes, and the name was taken as Greek 'aornos', 'birdless' (see 242). So the doves fly up, 'tollunt se', to clear the reek. 'Aëra' is a Greek accusative, with Greenough's diaeresis. 'Lapsae' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'labor', 'having glided'. 'Sedibus optatis' is 'on the longed-for seat', and 'geminae' is 'the pair'. 'Discolor' is 'of a different colour' from the green; 'auri… aura' plays on the two words, 'aura' here being a breath of light, a gleam. 'Refulsit' is a perfect, 'flashed out'.

sentences.t:
Quale solet silvis brumali frigore viscum
fronde virere nova, quod non sua seminat arbos,
et croceo fetu teretis circumdare truncos,
talis erat species auri frondentis opaca
ilice, sic leni crepitabat brattea vento.
sentences.l:
As in the woods in midwinter cold the mistletoe is wont
to be green with new leaf, which its own tree does not sow,
and with saffron fruit to wrap round the rounded trunks,
such was the look of the gold in leaf on the shady
holm-oak, so in the gentle wind rustled the foil.
sentences.i: As in the woods in the cold of midwinter the mistletoe puts out fresh green leaves, though no tree of its own has sown it, and wraps the rounded trunks with its saffron berries, such was the look of the gold leafing on the shadowy holm-oak, so did the thin gold leaf rustle in the light breeze.
sentences.n: An epic simile in the usual form, 'quale… talis', 'as… such': mistletoe, green in midwinter, is like the golden bough, alive on a tree that did not grow it. 'Brumali frigore' is 'in the cold of the winter solstice', midwinter. 'Viscum' is mistletoe, the subject of 'solet', which takes two infinitives, 'virere' and 'circumdare'. 'Quod non sua seminat arbos' is 'which not its own tree sows': mistletoe lives on its host but does not spring from it. 'Arbos' is the old form of 'arbor', which Greenough keeps. 'Croceo fetu' is 'with saffron-yellow fruit'; 'teretis… truncos' has the accusative plural in '-is', 'rounded trunks'. 'Auri frondentis' is 'of gold putting out leaves'; 'opaca ilice' is 'on the shady holm-oak', an ablative of place. 'Brattea' is gold leaf, metal beaten thin, and 'crepitabat' is 'rattled', 'rustled'.

sentences.t:
Corripit Aeneas extemplo avidusque refringit
cunctantem, et vatis portat sub tecta Sibyllae.
sentences.l:
Seizes it Aeneas at once, and eagerly breaks it off
as it lingers, and to the seer's roof carries it, the Sibyl's.
sentences.i: At once Aeneas seized it, broke it off eagerly though it clung, and carried it to the dwelling of the prophetess, the Sibyl.
sentences.n: 'Corripit' is 'snatches', the verb first for speed, and 'extemplo' is 'immediately'. 'Avidus' is again an adjective for an adverb, 'eagerly'. 'Refringit' is 'breaks off'. 'Cunctantem' is the bough 'lingering', 'holding back', though the Sibyl said it would follow 'willing and easy' if the fates called (146–147); readers have long asked whether the word only measures his eagerness against its toughness, or hints at something more. 'Vatis… Sibyllae' is 'of the seer, the Sibyl', set round 'portat sub tecta'. 'Tecta' is 'roofs', a dwelling.

sentences.t:
Nec minus interea Misenum in litore Teucri
flebant, et cineri ingrato suprema ferebant.
sentences.l:
Nor less meanwhile Misenus on the shore the Teucrians
were weeping, and to the thankless ash the last rites were bringing.
sentences.i: Meanwhile, no less, the Trojans on the shore were weeping for Misenus and paying the last honours to the ash that could not thank them.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Nec minus interea' is 'meanwhile, and no less', while Aeneas finds the bough. 'Teucri' are the Trojans, named from Teucer, an early king; the 'eu' is one syllable. 'Cineri ingrato' is 'to the thankless ash', the dead man who can no longer feel or give thanks, a dative; 'suprema' (neuter plural) are 'the last things', the funeral rites. The funeral that follows is modelled on Homer's funeral of Patroclus in Iliad 23 (the timber, the pyre, the wine on the embers, the bones gathered), and the crewman buried with his oar on his tomb on Elpenor in Odyssey 11–12.

sentences.t:
Principio pinguem taedis et robore secto
ingentem struxere pyram, cui frondibus atris
intexunt latera, et ferales ante cupressos
constituunt, decorantque super fulgentibus armis.
sentences.l:
First, rich with pine-brands and cut oak,
a huge pyre they built, whose with dark leaves
they interweave the sides, and funereal cypresses in front
set up, and adorn it on top with gleaming arms.
sentences.i: First they built a huge pyre, rich with resinous pine and split oak, wove its sides with dark leaves, set funeral cypresses before it, and crowned it with shining arms.
sentences.n: 'Principio' is 'first'. 'Pinguem taedis et robore secto' is 'rich with pine-torch wood and cut oak': 'taeda' is resinous pine, quick to burn. 'Struxere' is 'struxerunt'. 'Cui… intexunt latera' is 'whose sides they interweave', 'cui' a dative of reference where English uses a possessive. 'Frondibus atris' is 'with dark foliage'. Cypress, 'ferales… cupressos', is the tree of mourning, set before a Roman house of the dead; 'ferales' is 'funereal'. 'Super' is an adverb, 'above', and 'fulgentibus armis' are the dead man's arms, burned with him as in Homer.

sentences.t:
Pars calidos latices et aëna undantia flammis
expediunt, corpusque lavant frigentis et unguunt.
sentences.l:
Some warm waters and cauldrons surging from the flames
make ready, and the body they wash of the cold one, and anoint.
sentences.i: Some made ready hot water and bronze cauldrons seething over the fire, and washed and anointed the cold body.
sentences.n: 'Pars' is 'a part', 'some', a collective noun with a plural verb, 'expediunt', 'get ready'. 'Latices' are 'liquids', here water. 'Aëna' is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, 'bronze things', cauldrons; 'undantia flammis' is 'surging, boiling up, from the flames'. 'Corpus… frigentis' is 'the body of the cold one', 'frigentis' a genitive participle. Washing and anointing the body is Roman custom, and Homer's too (Patroclus in Iliad 18).

sentences.t: Fit gemitus.
sentences.l: There is a groaning.
sentences.i: A cry of mourning went up.
sentences.n: Two words and a full stop: 'fit gemitus', 'a groan arises', the ritual lament raised over the body. 'Fit' is from 'fio', 'happen', 'come about'.

sentences.t:
Tum membra toro defleta reponunt,
purpureasque super vestes, velamina nota,
coniciunt.
sentences.l:
Then the limbs, wept over, on the couch they lay back,
and purple over them robes, coverings well known,
they throw.
sentences.i: Then they laid the mourned body back upon the bier and cast over it purple robes, the garments he had worn.
sentences.n: 'Membra… defleta' is 'the limbs wept over', the perfect participle of 'defleo'; 'toro' is 'on the couch', the bier, a dative or ablative of place; 'reponunt' is 'lay back', 'lay to rest'. 'Super' is an adverb again, 'over (him)'. 'Velamina nota' is in apposition to 'vestes': 'familiar coverings', the clothes he wore in life. The verb 'coniciunt' runs over into the next line and ends the sentence.

sentences.t:
Pars ingenti subiere feretro,
triste ministerium, et subiectam more parentum
aversi tenuere facem.
sentences.l:
Some to the huge went under bier,
a sad service, and, set beneath, in the way of their fathers,
turned away they held the torch.
sentences.i: Some shouldered the great bier — a mournful office — and, as their fathers did, held the torch beneath the pyre with their faces turned away.
sentences.n: 'Subiere' and 'tenuere' are '-ere' perfects for '-erunt'. 'Ingenti… feretro' is a dative after the compound 'subeo', 'went under the huge bier', to lift it. 'Triste ministerium' is in apposition to the whole act, 'a sad service'. 'Subiectam… facem' is 'the torch put beneath' the pyre; 'more parentum' is 'in the custom of their ancestors'; 'aversi' is 'turned away', since by Roman custom the kin lit the pyre with face averted, not looking on death.

sentences.t:
Congesta cremantur
turea dona, dapes, fuso crateres olivo.
sentences.l:
Heaped together are burned
offerings of incense, viands, bowls with poured olive-oil.
sentences.i: The heaped offerings were burned — gifts of incense, food, and bowls of poured olive oil.
sentences.n: 'Congesta… turea dona' is 'heaped gifts of incense', the subject of 'cremantur', 'are burned'; 'dapes' are 'feast-dishes', food for the dead. 'Fuso crateres olivo' is 'bowls with poured oil', 'olivo' (from 'olivum') an ablative of description. 'Crateres' is a Greek nominative plural, mixing-bowls. The list runs on without 'and' (asyndeton).

sentences.t:
Postquam conlapsi cineres et flamma quievit
reliquias vino et bibulam lavere favillam,
ossaque lecta cado texit Corynaeus aëno.
sentences.l:
After the ashes fell in and the flame grew still,
the remains with wine and the thirsty they washed embers,
and the bones, gathered, in an urn laid away Corynaeus, of bronze.
sentences.i: When the ashes had sunk and the flame was still, they drenched the remains and the thirsty embers with wine, and Corynaeus gathered the bones and laid them away in a bronze urn.
sentences.n: 'Conlapsi' (Greenough's spelling of 'collapsi') is 'fell in', with 'sunt' left out. 'Reliquias' is 'the remains', its first syllable long, as if spelt 'relliquias', a licence Virgil takes with this word. 'Bibulam… favillam' is 'the thirsty ember-ash', which drinks the wine; 'lavere' is 'laverunt', 'washed'. 'Ossa… lecta' is 'the bones, gathered', 'lecta' from 'lego'. 'Cado… aëno' is 'in a bronze jar', framing the name; 'texit' is 'covered', 'stored away'. Quenching the pyre with wine and gathering the bones into an urn is what the Greeks do for Patroclus in Iliad 23.

sentences.t:
Idem ter socios pura circumtulit unda,
spargens rore levi et ramo felicis olivae,
lustravitque viros, dixitque novissima verba.
sentences.l:
The same man three times round the comrades carried pure water,
sprinkling with light dew and with a bough of fruitful olive,
and purified the men, and spoke the last words.
sentences.i: He too carried pure water three times round the company, sprinkling them with light drops from a branch of fruitful olive, purified the men, and spoke the final words of farewell.
sentences.n: 'Idem' is 'the same man', Corynaeus. 'Circumtulit' is 'carried round': 'circumferre' is the ritual word for purifying by carrying water round, here with 'socios' as object and 'pura… unda' as the means, 'carried pure water round the comrades'. 'Ter' is three times, the sacred number. 'Rore levi… et ramo' is 'with light dew and with a bough', the sprinkling done with the bough; 'felicis' is 'fruitful', its old sense. 'Lustravit' is 'purified', since those who touch the dead are polluted. 'Novissima verba' are 'the last words', the closing words of the rite: the farewell to the dead, or (as some old commentators took it) the formula that dismissed the mourners.

sentences.t:
At pius Aeneas ingenti mole sepulcrum
imponit, suaque arma viro, remumque tubamque,
monte sub aërio, qui nunc “Misenus ”ab illo
dicitur, aeternumque tenet per saecula nomen.
sentences.l:
But dutiful Aeneas with a huge mass a tomb
sets up, and his own gear for the man, both oar and trumpet,
beneath a soaring height, which now “Misenus” after him
is called, and an everlasting through the ages holds name.
sentences.i: But loyal Aeneas raised over him a tomb, a massive mound, and set on it the man's own gear, his oar and trumpet, beneath a lofty headland which is called Misenus after him now, and keeps an undying name through the ages.
sentences.n: The print has '“Misenus ”ab', a misprint for '“Misenus” ab', corrected here. The closing mark is set after a space and joined to the next word; t keeps the print, while l closes the quotation after 'Misenus'. 'At' marks the turn to Aeneas, 'pius' as always. 'Ingenti mole' is 'with a huge mass', an ablative of description with 'sepulcrum' (spelled so here; at 152 Greenough has 'sepulchro'). 'Sua… arma' is 'his own gear', 'sua' pointing to 'viro', Misenus; 'remumque tubamque' has the double '-que', 'both oar and trumpet'. The oar planted on the tomb is Elpenor's in Odyssey 11–12. 'Monte sub aërio' is 'under an airy height'; the headland is Cape Misenum on the bay of Naples, under Augustus the chief base of the Roman fleet. 'Qui… dicitur' gives the origin of the name, and 'aeternum' is 'everlasting'.

sentences.t: His actis, propere exsequitur praecepta Sibyllae.
sentences.l: These things done, swiftly he carries out the instructions of the Sibyl.
sentences.i: This done, he lost no time in carrying out the Sibyl's instructions.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'His actis' is an ablative absolute, 'these things having been done'. 'Propere' is 'quickly'; 'exsequitur' (a deponent) is 'carries out', 'follows through', and 'praecepta' are her instructions at 152–153: bury the friend, then bring black victims.

sentences.t:
Spelunca alta fuit vastoque immanis hiatu,
scrupea, tuta lacu nigro nemorumque tenebris,
quam super haud ullae poterant impune volantes
tendere iter pennis—talis sese halitus atris
faucibus effundens supera ad convexa ferebat:
sentences.l:
A deep cave there was, monstrous with its vast gape,
rugged, guarded by a black lake and the darkness of groves,
over which not any could unharmed flying things
hold their way on wings — such a breath, itself from the black
jaws pouring out, to the vault above was rising:
sentences.i: There was a deep cave, enormous, gaping wide, rough with jagged rock, guarded by a black lake and the darkness of the forest; no bird could fly over it and live, so deadly was the breath that poured from that black throat and rose to the dome of the sky:
sentences.n: A set description, opened in the usual way, 'there was a place': 'spelunca alta fuit'. 'Vasto… immanis hiatu' is 'monstrous with vast gaping', an ablative of description. 'Scrupea' is a rare word, 'full of sharp stones'. 'Tuta' is 'protected', with 'lacu… tenebris' as ablatives of means. 'Quam super' is 'over which', the preposition after its object. 'Volantes' is a participle used as a noun, 'flying things', birds, feminine with 'ullae' ('aves' understood). 'Impune' is 'without harm'. Greenough's dash, printed with no space, opens the reason, so the sentence is kept whole: 'talis… halitus' is 'such a breath', the poisonous vapour; 'sese' serves both 'effundens' and 'ferebat': pouring itself out, it 'carried itself', that is rose, 'supera ad convexa', 'to the vault above', the sky.

sentences.i: [Hence the Greeks gave the place the name Aornos, the Birdless.] Here first the priestess set four black-backed bullocks in place and tipped wine over their brows;
sentences.n: Line 242 stands in brackets: Greenough prints it as spurious, as many editors do: it reads like a learned gloss on the lines before, explaining the name. It says the Greeks called the place 'Aornos', 'birdless'; 'Aornon' is a Greek accusative (the Latin Library prints 'Aornum'), and 'Grai' is 'the Greeks'. It is joined to this unit because the colon at 241 runs on past it into 'quattuor'. 'Nigrantis terga iuvencos' is 'bullocks black as to their backs': 'nigrantis' is an accusative plural in '-is', and 'terga' an accusative of respect, as with 'defixus lumina' at 156. Black victims go to the powers below, as the Sibyl ordered. 'Constituit' is 'sets in place', and the subject, 'sacerdos', the Sibyl, is held to the end. 'Invergit' is 'tips', pouring by turning the cup over, a rite for the gods below; 'vina' is a poetic plural. Behind the whole sacrifice stands Odysseus's offering at the edge of the land of the dead in Odyssey 11.

sentences.t:
et summas carpens media inter cornua saetas
ignibus imponit sacris, libamina prima,
voce vocans Hecaten, Caeloque Ereboque potentem.
sentences.l:
and the topmost, plucking them from between the horns, bristles
on the fires lays, the sacred ones, as first offerings,
with her voice calling Hecate, in Heaven and in Erebus mighty.
sentences.i: and plucking the topmost bristles from between the horns she laid them on the sacred fire as the first offerings, crying aloud on Hecate, mighty in Heaven and in Erebus.
sentences.n: 'Summas… saetas' is 'the topmost bristles', framing 'carpens media inter cornua', 'plucking in the middle between the horns'. Cutting hairs from the victim's forehead and throwing them in the fire opens a sacrifice in Homer too. 'Libamina prima' is in apposition, 'as first offerings'. 'Voce vocans' is a play on the root, 'calling with the voice', 'aloud'. 'Hecaten' is a Greek accusative; Hecate, goddess of crossroads, night and the dead, set the Sibyl over these groves (118). 'Caeloque Ereboque' has the double '-que' again, ablatives of place, 'in Heaven and in Erebus', the darkness under the earth.

sentences.t:
Supponunt alii cultros, tepidumque cruorem
suscipiunt pateris.
sentences.l:
Put beneath others the knives, and the warm blood
catch in bowls.
sentences.i: Others set knives to the throats and caught the warm blood in bowls.
sentences.n: 'Supponunt… cultros' is 'put knives beneath', to the throats, a ritual way of saying they cut them. 'Alii' is 'others', the attendants. 'Cruor' is blood that has been shed. 'Suscipiunt' is 'catch from beneath' (the Latin Library spells it 'succipiunt'); 'pateris' is an ablative of means, 'paterae' being shallow libation bowls.

sentences.t:
Ipse atri velleris agnam
Aeneas matri Eumenidum magnaeque sorori
ense ferit, sterilemque tibi. Proserpina, vaccam.
sentences.l:
He himself a lamb of black fleece,
Aeneas, for the mother of the Eumenides and her great sister
with the sword strikes, and a barren for you, Proserpina, heifer.
sentences.i: Aeneas himself struck down with his sword a black-fleeced lamb for the mother of the Furies and her mighty sister, and for you, Proserpina, a barren heifer.
sentences.n: The print has 'tibi. Proserpina', a misprint for 'tibi, Proserpina', corrected here: the full stop would cut the vocative off from its own clause. t keeps the print, while l and i read the comma. 'Atri velleris' is a genitive of description, 'of black fleece'. 'Matri Eumenidum' is Night, mother of the Furies (the 'Kindly Ones', a name used to avoid ill-omened speech); 'magnae… sorori' is her great sister, Earth (in Hesiod both Earth and Night are among the first powers to come into being). 'Ense ferit' is 'strikes with the sword'. 'Tibi, Proserpina' is an apostrophe, the poet turning to address the queen of the dead; a barren cow suits the goddess of a realm where nothing grows.

sentences.t:
Tum Stygio regi nocturnas inchoat aras,
et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis,
pingue superque oleum infundens ardentibus extis.
sentences.l:
Then for the Stygian king night altars he begins,
and whole lays bulls' flesh on the flames,
rich and over oil pouring on the burning entrails.
sentences.i: Then he set up altars by night to the Stygian king, laid whole carcasses of bulls on the flames, and poured rich oil over the burning entrails.
sentences.n: 'Stygio regi' is Dis, king of the realm of the Styx. 'Nocturnas… aras' are 'altars by night', since the gods below receive their offerings in the dark; 'inchoat' is 'begins', 'sets up' (the Latin Library spells it 'incohat'). 'Solida… viscera' is 'whole flesh', the carcasses unbroken: an offering to the gods below was burned entire, with no share for the worshippers. 'Pingue… oleum' is 'rich oil', with 'super' an adverb joined by '-que', 'and over (them)'; 'ardentibus extis' is a dative after 'infundens', 'pouring onto the burning inwards'.

sentences.t:
Ecce autem, primi sub lumina solis et ortus,
sub pedibus mugire solum, et iuga coepta moveri
silvarum, visaeque canes ululare per umbram,
adventante dea.
sentences.l:
But look, close upon the light of the first sun and its rising,
beneath their feet the ground bellowed, and the ridges began to stir
of the forests, and dogs seemed to howl through the gloom,
as the goddess drew near.
sentences.i: But see — just at the first light of the rising sun the ground began to rumble under their feet, the wooded ridges to stir, and hounds seemed to howl through the dusk as the goddess drew near.
sentences.n: 'Ecce autem' is 'but look!', a sudden turn. 'Sub lumina' is 'close upon the light', 'sub' with the accusative of time; 'primi… solis et ortus' is 'of the first sun and its rising', two ways of saying dawn. The Latin Library prints 'limina', 'the threshold of the first sun', another picture of the same moment. 'Mugire' is a historical infinitive, 'the ground bellowed'; 'coepta' and 'visae' have 'sunt' left out, 'began to be moved', 'seemed'. 'Canes' is feminine here ('visae'): hounds are Hecate's beasts, and their howling tells of her coming. 'Adventante dea' is an ablative absolute, 'the goddess approaching'.

sentences.t:
“Procul O procul este, profani,”
conclamat vates, “totoque absistite luco;
sentences.l:
“Far, O far off be, you unhallowed,”
cries out the seer, “and from the whole stand away grove;
sentences.i: “Keep off, keep far off, all you who are not initiated,” the seer cried, “and stand clear of the whole grove;
sentences.n: The opening mark begins the Sibyl's words, broken by 'conclamat vates' and closed at 261. 'Procul este, profani' is the cry that cleared the ground before a mystery rite: 'profani' are those outside the 'fanum', the shrine, the uninitiated, here Aeneas's companions. 'Este' is the plural imperative of 'sum'. 'Conclamat' is 'cries aloud'. 'Absistite' is 'stand away', with 'toto… luco' an ablative of separation.

sentences.t: tuque invade viam, vaginaque eripe ferrum:
sentences.l: and you, rush upon the road, and from the sheath snatch the sword:
sentences.i: but you, set out upon the road and pluck your sword from its sheath:
sentences.n: 'Tuque' is Aeneas, the one exception. 'Invade viam' is 'go in upon the way', 'set boldly on the road'. 'Vagina' is an ablative of separation, 'from the sheath', and 'eripe' is 'snatch out'. In Odyssey 11 Odysseus draws his sword to keep the shades from the blood; here the sword is a sign of courage, and the end of this part shows it will be no use.

sentences.t: nunc animis opus, Aenea, nunc pectore firmo.”
sentences.l: now of courage there is need, Aeneas, now of a steady heart.”
sentences.i: now you need your courage, Aeneas, now a steadfast heart.”
sentences.n: 'Opus' with an ablative is 'there is need of', with 'est' left out: 'animis', 'courage' (the plural of 'animus' means spirit, mettle), and 'pectore firmo', 'a firm breast'. 'Aenea' is a Greek vocative. The closing mark ends the Sibyl's speech.

sentences.t: Tantum effata, furens antro se immisit aperto;
sentences.l: So much having spoken, raving, into the cave she flung herself, the open one;
sentences.i: So much she said, and in her frenzy flung herself into the open cave;
sentences.n: 'Tantum effata' is 'having spoken so much', the participle of the deponent 'effor' (as at 197). 'Furens' is 'raving', still possessed by the god. 'Se immisit' is 'sent herself in', 'plunged'; 'antro… aperto' is a dative with the compound verb, 'into the open cave'.

sentences.t: ille ducem haud timidis vadentem passibus aequat.
sentences.l: he his guide, with not timid steps going, keeps level with.
sentences.i: and he, with no faltering step, kept pace with his guide as she went.
sentences.n: 'Ille' is Aeneas. 'Aequat' is 'equals', 'keeps up with', and its object is 'ducem… vadentem', 'his guide as she goes'. 'Haud timidis… passibus' is a litotes, 'with steps not timid', that is bold ones; it can go with 'aequat' (he matches her with bold steps) or with 'vadentem' (she strides boldly, and he keeps up).

sentences.i: Gods whose rule is over the souls of the dead, and you silent shades, and Chaos, and Phlegethon, broad tracts hushed in night: may heaven's law allow me to tell what I have heard;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the poet's own voice: before the descent he calls on the powers below, as epic poets call on the Muses before a great undertaking. 'Quibus imperium est' is a dative of possession, 'to whom belongs the rule'. 'Chaos' is the first void, from which came Erebus and Night in Hesiod; 'Phlegethon' is the river of fire in the underworld, its name Greek for 'blazing'. 'Loca… tacentia late' is in apposition, 'places silent far and wide'. 'Sit… fas' is a subjunctive of wish, 'may it be right' by divine law; 'audita' is 'things heard', a neuter plural participle, as if the poet were passing on what was told to the initiated.

sentences.t:
sit numine vestro
pandere res alta terra et caligine mersas!
sentences.l:
may it be, by your divine will,
to lay open things in deep earth and darkness sunk!
sentences.i: may I, by your leave, lay bare what lies sunk deep in the earth and the dark!
sentences.n: 'Sit' repeats the wish, with 'fas' understood. 'Numine vestro' is 'by your will', an ablative of accordance: 'numen' is the nod, the power of a god. 'Pandere' is 'to spread open', 'reveal'. 'Res… mersas' is 'things sunk', with 'alta terra et caligine' set inside it; 'alta' goes with 'terra', 'deep earth'.

sentences.t:
Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbram,
perque domos Ditis vacuas et inania regna:
sentences.l:
They were going, dim, under the lonely night through the shadow,
and through the halls of Dis, empty, and the void kingdoms:
sentences.i: Unseen they walked under the lonely night through the gloom, through the vacant halls of Dis and his kingdom of empty things:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. One of the most admired lines in Virgil turns on a transferred epithet (as with 'memorem' at I.4): 'obscuri sola sub nocte' is 'dark under the lonely night', where plain sense would give 'alone under the dark night'; the two adjectives have traded places, and each still works where it stands. 'Ibant' is an imperfect, 'they were going', a long walk. 'Domos Ditis' are 'the halls of Dis'; 'vacuas' and 'inania' are 'empty', 'void', a realm of bodiless things. The colon leads into a simile.

sentences.t:
quale per incertam lunam sub luce maligna
est iter in silvis, ubi caelum condidit umbra
Iuppiter, et rebus nox abstulit atra colorem.
sentences.l:
as by an uncertain moon under a grudging light
is a journey in woods, when the sky has hidden in shadow
Jupiter, and from things black night has taken their colour.
sentences.i: like a road through the woods by a fitful moon in its niggardly light, when Jupiter has buried the sky in shadow and black night has drained all things of their colour.
sentences.n: 'Quale… est iter' is 'such as is a journey', the relative introducing the comparison. 'Per incertam lunam' is 'by an uncertain moon', hazed or half-hidden; 'luce maligna' is 'a grudging light', 'malignus' meaning stingy as well as spiteful. 'Ubi… condidit' is 'when he has hidden', a perfect of what happens at any time. Jupiter is the sky-god, master of weather, so 'caelum condidit umbra Iuppiter' is 'Jupiter has buried the sky in shadow'. 'Rebus' is a dative of separation with 'abstulit', 'has taken away from things'.

sentences.t:
Vestibulum ante ipsum, primisque in faucibus Orci
Luctus et ultrices posuere cubilia Curae;
sentences.l:
Before the forecourt itself, and in the first jaws of Orcus,
Grief and avenging have set their beds Cares;
sentences.i: Before the very entrance, in the outer throat of Orcus, Grief and the avenging Cares have made their beds;
sentences.n: 'Vestibulum ante ipsum' is 'ante ipsum vestibulum', the preposition set between noun and adjective. The 'vestibulum' is the forecourt of a Roman house, the open space before the door where callers waited, and 'fauces' is also the word for the narrow passage into a house, so the underworld is pictured as a great man's mansion with its hangers-on at the door. 'Orci' is Orcus, an old Roman name for the god of death and his realm. 'Luctus' and 'Curae' are personified, and Greenough capitalises them: 'ultrices… Curae' are 'avenging Cares', the pangs of conscience. 'Posuere' is 'posuerunt'. The list that follows draws on Hesiod's catalogue of the children of Night and of Strife in the Theogony.

sentences.t:
pallentesque habitant Morbi, tristisque Senectus,
et Metus, et malesuada Fames, ac turpis Egestas,
terribiles visu formae:
sentences.l:
and pale dwell Diseases, and grim Old Age,
and Fear, and ill-counselling Hunger, and foul Want,
terrible to see shapes:
sentences.i: pale Diseases dwell there, and grim Old Age, and Fear, and Hunger that counsels crime, and degrading Want, shapes terrible to look on:
sentences.n: More personifications, each with its epithet. 'Pallentes… Morbi' is 'pale Diseases'. 'Malesuada' is 'evil-persuading', a compound of 'male' and 'suadeo': hunger drives men to crime. 'Turpis Egestas' is 'shameful Want', poverty that degrades. 'Terribiles visu formae' is in apposition, 'shapes terrible to see': 'visu' is the supine in '-u', an ablative of respect, as in 'mirabile dictu'.

sentences.t: Letumque, Labosque;
sentences.l: and Death, and Toil;
sentences.i: and Death, and Toil;
sentences.n: 'Letum' is 'death', the poetic word, and 'Labos' is the old form of 'labor', 'toil', which Greenough keeps (like 'arbos' at 206). The double '-que' carries the list on.

sentences.t:
tum consanguineus Leti Sopor, et mala mentis
Gaudia, mortiferumque adverso in limine Bellum,
ferreique Eumenidum thalami, et Discordia demens,
vipereum crinem vittis innexa cruentis.
sentences.l:
then the blood-kin of Death, Sleep, and the evil of the mind
Joys, and death-bringing on the threshold opposite War,
and the iron chambers of the Eumenides, and Discord mad,
her viper hair with ribbons bound, bloodstained ones.
sentences.i: then Sleep, of one blood with Death, and the guilty Joys of the mind, and on the threshold facing them death-dealing War, and the iron chambers of the Furies, and mad Discord, her viper hair bound up with bloodstained ribbons.
sentences.n: 'Consanguineus Leti Sopor' is 'Sleep, of one blood with Death': in Homer and Hesiod Sleep and Death are twin brothers, sons of Night. 'Mala mentis Gaudia' are 'the evil joys of the mind', guilty pleasures, with 'Gaudia' carried over to the next line. 'Adverso in limine' is 'on the threshold opposite'. 'Ferrei' is two syllables, 'e' and 'i' run together (synizesis); the 'thalami', 'bedchambers', of the Furies are of iron. 'Discordia' is the Greek Eris, Strife. 'Vipereum crinem… innexa' is a passive participle with a direct object, 'having bound her viper-hair', the Greek middle use; 'vittae' are the woollen fillets worn by priestesses and victims, here soaked in blood.

sentences.t:
In medio ramos annosaque brachia pandit
ulmus opaca, ingens, quam sedem Somnia volgo
vana tenere ferunt, foliisque sub omnibus haerent.
sentences.l:
In the midst its boughs and aged arms spreads
an elm, shady, huge, which as their seat Dreams everywhere,
empty ones, hold, they say, and under all the leaves they cling.
sentences.i: In the middle an elm, huge and dark, stretches out its branches and its aged arms; there, men say, idle Dreams roost everywhere, hanging beneath each leaf.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'In medio' is 'in the middle' of the forecourt. 'Ramos annosaque brachia' is 'branches and aged arms', two words for one thing; 'brachia' is Greenough's spelling ('bracchia' in the Latin Library). 'Quam sedem… tenere ferunt' is 'which as a seat (they) hold, men say', with 'ferunt', 'they say', taking an accusative and infinitive. 'Somnia… vana' are 'empty Dreams', held apart across the line-end. 'Volgo' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulgo', 'everywhere', 'in crowds'. The dreams come back at the end of the book, at the twin gates of Sleep, which go back to the gates of horn and ivory in Odyssey 19.

sentences.t: Multaque praeterea variarum monstra ferarum:
sentences.l: And many besides, of various beasts, monsters:
sentences.i: And there are many monstrous beasts of every kind besides:
sentences.n: The verb is left out ('sunt', 'there are'). 'Monstra' are 'portents', 'monsters', with 'variarum… ferarum' framing the line, 'of beasts of various kinds'. The colon opens the list.

sentences.t:
Centauri in foribus stabulant, Scyllaeque biformes,
et centumgeminus Briareus, ac belua Lernae
horrendum stridens, flammisque armata Chimaera,
Gorgones Harpyiaeque et forma tricorporis umbrae.
sentences.l:
Centaurs at the doors are stalled, and two-formed Scyllas,
and hundredfold Briareus, and the beast of Lerna
horribly hissing, and armed with flames the Chimaera,
Gorgons and Harpies, and the shape of the three-bodied shade.
sentences.i: Centaurs have their stalls at the doors, and Scyllas, half girl, half beast, and Briareus with his hundred arms, the Lernaean monster with its fearful hiss, the Chimaera bristling with fire, Gorgons and Harpies, and the ghost of the giant with three bodies.
sentences.n: 'Stabulant' is 'are stalled', 'have their stables', fitting the horse-bodied Centaurs. 'Scyllae biformes' are Scyllas, the plural for the kind, 'two-formed', a girl above and a sea-beast ringed with dogs below, as at III.426–432 (Homer's Scylla in Odyssey 12 is a different creature, with six heads on long necks). 'Centumgeminus Briareus' is 'hundredfold Briareus', the hundred-handed giant of Iliad 1. 'Belua Lernae' is the Hydra of Lerna, killed by Hercules; 'horrendum stridens' has 'horrendum' as an adverbial accusative, like 'grave olentis' at 201. The Chimaera, lion, goat and snake breathing fire, is Homer's too (Iliad 6). 'Gorgones Harpyiaeque' are the snake-haired Gorgons and the Harpies, whom the Trojans fought in Book III. 'Forma tricorporis umbrae' is 'the shape of the three-bodied shade', Geryon, whose cattle Hercules drove off.

sentences.t:
Corripit hic subita trepidus formidine ferrum
Aeneas, strictamque aciem venientibus offert,
et, ni docta comes tenues sine corpore vitas
admoneat volitare cava sub imagine formae,
inruat, et frustra ferro diverberet umbras.
sentences.l:
Snatches here, in sudden terror alarmed, his sword
Aeneas, and the drawn edge to them as they come presents,
and, had not his knowing companion that thin lives without body
flit under a hollow semblance of form warned him,
he would rush in, and in vain with the sword would cleave shadows.
sentences.i: Here, shaken by sudden terror, Aeneas snatched up his sword and turned its bare edge on them as they came; and had not his wise companion warned him that these were frail lives with no bodies, fluttering about in the empty likeness of a shape, he would have charged them and hacked uselessly at shadows with his blade.
sentences.n: 'Corripit' opens the line as it did at 210, when he seized the bough. 'Subita… formidine' is 'with sudden fear', framing 'trepidus', 'alarmed'. 'Strictam aciem' is 'the drawn edge'; 'venientibus' is a dative participle, 'to them as they come'. 'Ni… admoneat… inruat… diverberet' is a condition contrary to fact put in the present subjunctive, where prose would use the pluperfect: the present keeps the danger before our eyes. 'Docta comes' is the Sibyl, 'knowing' about this world. 'Tenues sine corpore vitas… volitare' is an accusative and infinitive after 'admoneat', 'that thin lives without body flit'; 'cava sub imagine formae' is 'under the hollow likeness of a shape'. 'Inruat' is Greenough's spelling of 'irruat'. Odysseus too draws his sword among the dead in Odyssey 11, and clutches three times in vain at his mother's shade.
